nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What was the primary focus of the research mentioned in the abstract?
nodes.answer: The primary focus was to investigate whether the use of learning gardens in initial teacher training impacts students' connectedness to nature.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract It is well known that the relationship between humans and nature conditions peo - ple S pro-environmental behaviours, as well as being one of the keys to developing sustainability. The focus of this research is whether the use of learning gardens in initial teacher training has an impact on students connectedness to nature. The study follows a quasi-experimental design, involving 84 students from the Undergraduate Degree in Early Childhood Education distributed into a control group ( n = 36) and a treatment group ( n = 48). The participants completed two quantitative scales (INS and NEP-R) before and after an educational intervention that took place over a four- month academic period. The findings show that, after instruction, both groups had improved their relationship with nature. Specifically, their environmental concern had increased after the training, but the impact was only significant in the group who used the garden. On the other hand, regarding the self-nature connection, no significant changes were observed in any of the two groups. This strengthens the idea that connectedness to nature is a primitive belief that, although hard to modify in adulthood, can be improved through certain actions.

nodes.question: What are the prospects mentioned for the use of learning gardens in the training of pre-service teachers?
nodes.answer: The use of learning gardens opens different prospects for enhancing the training of pre-service teachers by promoting environmental awareness and education.

Keywords Pre-service teachers School gardens Learning gardens Connectedness to nature Environmental concernAccepted: 24 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025Connectedness to nature: assessing the impact of garden- based learning on teacher education Diego Corrochano Fern ndez1 Alejandro G mez-Gon alves1 Sara Serrate Gonz lez1 Jos Manuel Mu OZ Rodr guez1 Diego Corrochano Fern ndez dcf@usal.es Alejandro G mez-Gon alves algomez@usal.es Sara Serrate Gonz lez sarasg@usal.es Jos Manuel Mu OZ Rodr guez pepema@usal.es 1 Universidad de Salamanca, Salamanca, Spain 13 Journal of Outdoor and Environmental EducationIntroduction The planet is facing a global environmental crisis that is mainly linked to the effects of climate change, pollution, and biodiversity loss. To ensure a sustainable future requires a joint and systematic approach to these problems. In this regard, educa - tion is essential to the political and economic transformation that is needed (Baste et al., 2021 ). Despite the efforts engaged in over the last decades, education for sus - tainability and environmental education as genuine training for sustainable devel - opment still require improvement, since the future of our environment depends on the decisions made by future generations (Murga-Menoyo, 2021 ).

nodes.label: Education and Training
nodes.question: How can learning gardens impact teacher training in environmental education?
nodes.answer: The use of learning gardens in the university system can play an important role in fostering environmentally friendly values in initial teacher training.
nodes.paragraph: Different stud - ies have highlighted the importance of teacher training in environmental issues as a crucial component to ensure that teachers in their professional future may approach socio-environmental sustainability competences with their students (Varela-Losada et al., 2019 ). Nevertheless, previous studies have also reported deficiencies regard - ing education for sustainable development and socio-environmental topics in initial teacher training (Morote et al., 2021 ), as well as among teachers in service (Borg et al., 2013 ). There is clear evidence of the need to enhance teacher training in these areas, ensuring they feel both competent and confident in introducing environmental education programs. This will help foster behaviours that promote interaction with and care for the environment, as well as environmentally friendly values, beliefs, and attitudes. In this sense, the use of learning gardens in the university system as teach - ing resources could play an important role in fostering these values in initial teacher training (V zquez-Verdera & Esc mez-S inchez, 2022 ). The basis of current environmental problems lies in people S environmental cul - ture (Moyano-Diaz et al., 2011 ).

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: Why is it important for schools to engage in education about and in nature?
nodes.answer: It is essential for schools to engage in education about and in nature to provide opportunities for students to connect with nature from an early age, influencing their environmental actions in adulthood.
nodes.paragraph: Despite the many positive aspects it entails, contact with nature is ever scarcer in European countries, where most of the population lives in cities (The World Bank, 2023 ). The increase in indoor activities, the pace of life, the use of video games, and online relationships, especially among young people and children, are alarmingly increasing this disconnection from nature (Larson et al., 2018 ). Hence, it is essential for schools to engage in education about and in nature, offering opportunities to con - nect with it from the earliest ages. This would be a path to influence the environmen - tal actions that students will implement in adulthood (Chawla, 2012 ). It should also be noted that former research suggests that bonds to the natural world are usually formed in childhood (Chawla, 1998 ). Even secondary school students can be too old to experience affective changes in their connection with nature (Ernst & Theimer, 2011 ). This, therefore, leads to the question of which strategies are the most appropri - ate to foster greater connectedness with nature in adults.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why might secondary school students struggle to experience affective changes in their connection with nature?
nodes.answer: Secondary school students may be too old to experience affective changes in their connection with nature, as significant bonds are typically established in early childhood.
